Share on X Telegram The future of Nvidia chief executive officer, Jensen Huang, has come under fresh scrutiny as the board of the world’s largest artificial intelligence chipmaker considers his position following reports of two extramarital relationships, raising concerns about corporate governance, investor confidence and the financial stability of the global AI industry.
The board reportedly met on Wednesday to discuss Huang’s future after fresh allegations emerged, including a reported relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice-president of healthcare. The allegations followed an earlier controversy involving Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman reportedly suspected by US intelligence officials of having links to Beijing.
According to Reuters, the board’s deliberations represent a significant development, particularly after it had earlier expressed confidence in Huang. The company has since initiated an independent investigation, with external legal advisers engaged to examine the allegations and their possible implications for national security and corporate governance.
Huang, 63, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, has acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to employees but has not provided details of the relationships. He has also pledged to cooperate with the investigation.
The controversy has triggered significant market concerns, with Nvidia reportedly losing about $600 billion in market value since the investigation began. Its shares also fell sharply following reports that the board was considering Huang’s possible removal, while investment analysts have raised concerns about the company’s leadership uncertainty.
The financial implications extend beyond Nvidia’s shareholders. As the dominant supplier of advanced processors used in artificial intelligence systems, the company’s fortunes are closely linked to investments in data centres, cloud computing, semiconductor manufacturing and AI infrastructure worldwide.
However, it is reported that investors were particularly concerned about whether a leadership change could affect Nvidia’s strategy of financing and supporting major AI infrastructure projects. The company has disclosed financial commitments of about $164.5 billion, including obligations relating to data centre development and capacity arrangements.
Companies benefiting from Nvidia’s investments and technology have also faced market pressure. Shares of data-centre operator CoreWeave and South Korean internet company Naver declined following the latest developments, while some competing chipmakers, including Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom, recorded gains as investors reassessed the competitive landscape.
The uncertainty could also affect semiconductor supply chains across Asia, particularly manufacturers in Taiwan and South Korea that depend on Nvidia’s demand for advanced chips. Furthermore, renewed scrutiny of the alleged China connections could complicate US export-control policies and Nvidia’s access to one of the world’s largest technology markets.
Nvidia’s succession challenge is another concern, as Huang has not publicly identified a clear successor after more than three decades at the helm. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress and data-centre executive Ian Buck have been mentioned in succession discussions, although neither has Huang’s public profile or influence over the company’s strategic direction.
The controversy comes ahead of Nvidia’s November 17 earnings announcement, which investors will closely monitor for indications of its financial performance, future demand for AI processors and management’s response to the crisis.
Meanwhile, for the global technology markets, the unfolding situation represents more than a leadership dispute. Any prolonged disruption at Nvidia could influence investment decisions, AI infrastructure financing and the fortunes of companies whose business models increasingly depend on its chips.
